name: Silk (Bombyx mori), degummed, dyed and woven
summary: Cultivated silk: the fibroin filament the domesticated silkworm spins into its cocoon, degummed, dyed and woven. In the Salon it is the wall silk of the five bays, wrapped onto the faces of their piers, one colour to each bay, and the Manet cabinet's green; in Chenghuai it covers the cases' back panels and beds (a warm grey 绫) and the palace lanterns' panels, lit from within at night.

whyAnAccent.text: The material-language board groups the cloths with the timber: 'D · The oak, and what it carries: timber, leather, silk, felt'. Each cloth is declared an accent of the oak family (D-014); the Architect may overturn this reading.
whyAnAccent.source: MuseeVision/Journal/Decisions.md, D-014 (Matter: every substance carries its family; an accent names its core family); plan/canvas/MaterialsOther.dc.html, section 'D · The oak, and what it carries'

formation.how: The silkworm spins its cocoon from one continuous fibre: two fibroin filaments cemented in a sheath of sericin. The cocoons are reeled; the raw silk is degummed in hot soap or alkali, which strips the sericin and takes about a quarter of the weight, leaving the lustrous fibroin. The filaments are triangular to irregular in section, which is part of silk's sparkle. It is dyed in the yarn or the piece and woven: a plain taffeta; shantung and dupion, whose uneven, slubbed weft gives a broken, lively surface; a twill damask such as 绫; or an open gauze. Nineteenth-century silks were often 'weighted' with tin salts to replace the lost weight, and weighted silk shatters.

shantung.text: A silk plain weave, historically from Shandong; like dupioni but slightly thinner and less irregular; its yarns may have knots and bumps (slubs); a ribbed surface from long weft yarns.

optics.sheen: Each filament reflects on a cone about its axis; smooth, untwisted filaments (flat threads) give narrow, bright highlights and twisted threads broad ones. A slubbed weave breaks the highlight into short, irregular flashes.

sensitivity.text: High light sensitivity (ISO Blue Wool 1-3) covers most plant extracts and hence most historic bright dyes, insect dyes, most early synthetic colours, and textiles; UV causes yellowing, chalking and weakening, and prolonged exposure weakens and fragments most wool, cotton, silk and paper.

photograph: A slubbed weave: short thicker flecks along the weft that catch the light, so a flat wall of one colour still shimmers.
Colour that shifts a little with the angle of view; a paler sheen along the threads at grazing light.
Seams and the tension of stretched cloth: faint ripples near fixings, a crisp fold at each pier arris.
Faded edges and a paler band where a light slot or daylight has fallen for years; a sharp line of unfaded colour behind a frame.
